name: Basil
description: Sweet Basil is one of the most popular culinary herbs worldwide. Known for its distinct, fragrant aroma and sweet, slightly spicy cloves-and-anise flavor, it is the crowning glory of caprese salads and traditional Italian pesto.

growingConditions.watering: Moist, well-drained soil; water deeply when top inch is dry
growingConditions.soilType: Rich, loamy, well-draining soil with neutral pH

uses: Key ingredient in traditional Genovese pesto
Complements tomato dishes, pizzas, and fresh mozzarella
Infused in oils, vinegars, and herbal teas

video.title: How to Grow Basil (Complete Guide to Harvest)

uses: Traditionally taken as a tea to settle mild digestive upset and bloating
Leaves and oil used in folk remedies for minor inflammation and colds
Aroma commonly used to help lift mood and ease tension
benefits: Rich in vitamin K, which supports normal blood clotting and bone health
Contains antioxidants such as flavonoids and eugenol
Provides small amounts of vitamin A, manganese and iron
medicinal.caution: Basil is high in vitamin K, so people taking blood thinners such as warfarin should ask their doctor before eating large amounts.

taste: Sweet and fragrant with a peppery, clove-and-anise note.
sideEffects: Very large amounts may affect blood clotting because of the vitamin K
Concentrated basil oil or extract can irritate the stomach or skin
Rarely causes an allergic reaction in people sensitive to other mint-family plants

safety.allergy: Basil belongs to the mint family. People who react to mint, oregano or thyme may also react to basil. Stop using it if you get itching, a rash or swelling.
safety.pregnancy: Normal food amounts are considered safe. Avoid concentrated extracts and medicinal doses unless a doctor agrees.
safety.pets: Basil is generally regarded as non-toxic to cats and dogs, but large amounts can upset their stomach.
safety.medications: Basil is rich in vitamin K, so people taking blood thinners such as warfarin should keep their intake steady and ask their doctor.

temperature: Loves warmth: it grows best at about 18-30 °C. Cold below about 10 °C slows it down, and frost kills it. Plant outside only after the last frost.
harvest: Start picking when the plant has about six leaves, ideally in the morning. Pinch the stem just above a pair of leaves so two new shoots grow. Take no more than a third of the plant at once and remove flower buds to keep the leaves tasty.
storage: Do not put basil in the fridge, because cold turns the leaves black. Keep the stems in a glass of water on the counter for up to a week, or chop and freeze it in olive oil or ice cubes. Drying loses much of its flavor.
dailyLife: Tear fresh leaves over tomato salad, pizza or pasta just before serving
Blend into pesto with olive oil, nuts and cheese
Add to a cup of warm water or tea after a heavy meal
Keep a pot on the kitchen windowsill for easy picking
tips: Pinch off flower buds regularly to keep the plant bushy
Plant it near tomatoes, they like the same warm sunny spot
Water the soil rather than the leaves to avoid mildew

origin.details: Basil has been grown in India and tropical Asia for thousands of years. Traders carried it west to the Mediterranean, where it became the heart of Italian cooking.
